title: When strong is right
context: A public health student reports a large trial. Read the whole paragraph before you choose: this time the evidence is strong, and the writer is confident.
question: Which reporting verb fits best? Try more than one and compare what each says about the writer's view.
text: Missed vaccination appointments are a persistent problem in primary care. In a randomised controlled trial involving 4,000 patients across 30 GP practices, {{cite:adebayo2023|integral}} {{gap}} that a single text message reminder, sent two days before an appointment, increased attendance by twelve percentage points. Because the trial was large, randomised and carried out in ordinary practices rather than a research clinic, its result is likely to apply widely. A reminder system of this kind is also cheap to run, since each message costs very little to send. For practices looking for a low-cost way to improve uptake, the case for introducing text reminders is therefore strong.

options.signal: Endorsing. The writer accepts the finding as well established.
options.feedback: A strong choice here. The writer goes on to explain why the trial is trustworthy, so an endorsing verb is consistent with the rest of the paragraph.

options.signal: Endorsing. Presents the finding as established fact.
options.feedback: This works well. Strong verbs aren't a mistake in themselves: they are right when the evidence, and your own evaluation of it, justify them.

options.signal: Tentative. The evidence points one way, but the claim isn't settled.
options.feedback: Not wrong, but more cautious than the writer turns out to be. The paragraph ends by calling the case 'strong', so a tentative verb sits a little oddly with it.

options.signal: Neutral. Reports a position or interpretation.
options.feedback: 'Argues' suits an interpretation or a position. For a measured trial result, it makes the finding sound more like an opinion than it is.

options.signal: Distancing. Often signals that the writer doubts the source.
options.feedback: This clashes with the paragraph. 'Claims' hints that the writer is sceptical — then the next sentence explains why the result can be trusted.

options.signal: Concession. Implies the source reluctantly accepts something.
options.feedback: 'Admits' implies the authors conceded this against their own position. It's their main finding, so the verb gives the wrong impression.

notes.text: Compare this with 'A pinch of suggests' in the same module. There, the evidence was a survey of impressions and the writer was cautious, so 'suggests' fitted best. Here the evidence is a large trial, so a stronger verb fits. The right verb depends on the evidence and on what you, the writer, think of it.
APA recommends the past tense (demonstrated, showed) for reporting what a source found, so the verbs here appear in the past tense.

chefsNote: Sometimes a strong reporting verb is right. Check the evidence first.
